headlines.title: Credit stress is threatening to unwind the AI bull. All eyes are on Oracle to hold the line
headlines.summary: Investors are pushing up the cost of insurance against an Oracle default.
headlines.article_text: oracle-credit-default-swaps-ai-debt Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AI names like CoreWeave and Oracle were both hit on Friday. Unlike CoreWeave, Oracle is an investment-grade name. However, investors are pushing up the cost of insurance against an Oracle default. In this article ORCL CRWV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The New York Stock Exchange welcomes executives and guests of Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) to the podium on Sept. 9th, 2026. NYSE Oracle bonds are sitting dangerously close to junk territory as markets cool on artificial intelligence. Much of the AI trade fizzled last week, led by CoreWeave — the neocloud company whose equity and debt has been tanking . Oracle now faces risk of credit rating downgrades that could tip its debt into junk territory — with potentially cascading effects across the AI financing ecosystem. "There seems to be a sentiment shift, which almost speaks to 2026 in general, where we're so bullish about everything and then we're so bearish about everything," said Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners. "It just shows you how quickly this market moves." But there are key differences between CoreWeave and Oracle — the latter is investment grade while Coreweave is already in junk territory. Some analysts and fixed income investors tell CNBC they aren't concerned yet about Oracle and the other hyperscalers. Oracle year to date Still, the shift in sentiment can be seen in the spread of Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The range is more in line with BB and B credit, which is high yield, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The spread on Oracle's five-year CDS is currently 295 basis points, after briefly hitting 300 bps on Thursday, up 287% in one year. "Oracle CDS is supported by high liquidity. Nonetheless, its spreads whipsawed over the last few days, no doubt a reflection of the fragile sentiment in AI-related names, notably those in HY [high yield] and at the weaker end of the IG [investment-grade] spectrum, such as Oracle," he said in an email to CNBC. Oracle's 5-year credit default swaps Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CDS means investors view the debt as riskier. Oracle's rating is S&P Credit Ratings is BBB-, the lowest level in the investment-grade spectrum. The agency downgraded Oracle in July, noting that the company's rapidly expanding infrastructure business is increasing its overall credit risk. S&P also said it expects weaker operating cash flow in 2027. A 'bellwether' Oracle is primarily an enterprise software company but it's barreling into data centers and cloud services, including a massive $300 billion deal with OpenAI. To fund the buildout, Oracle has issued $118 billion in long-term debt and has another $39 billion in capital and lease obligations, according to FactSet data. The spending and debt obligations are taking a toll on Oracle's finances while the company waits for a gusher of AI revenue. Analysts estimate free cash flow of -$23.7 billion this year and -$36 billion in 2027, according to consensus forecasts. That would be bad enough for investors, but Oracle is more than just a debt-laden data center play. It's become an AI "bellwether," notes Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank. A downgrade of its credit into junk territory "would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," he said in a report. S&P said in its July downgrade that another downgrade could be triggered by: an expectation that Oracle will sustain leverage exceeding 4x; or belief that the software company isn't on a path to generate positive free operating cash flow by fiscal 2029; or a negative view on Oracle's AI strategy or that of the overall AI industry. As an investment-grade company, Oracle can borrow cheaply and with duration, but that would change with a junk rating, said Jamie Meyers, a senior securities analyst at Laffer Tengler, which owns Oracle stock. "Nobody in high yield is going to buy a 30 year debt," he said. "Getting downgraded to junk would mean that they'd have to push everything short. Obviously, their borrowing rate would be higher, more than likely." That said, Meyers is not concerned about Oracle's debt levels. In a meeting between Oracle and Laffer Tengler last year, Oracle stressed it will defend its investment-grade rating, Meyers said. "We do believe the revenue is going to start ramping and the earnings are going to start ramping," he said. "What Oracle really needs is … time. They need to get these things built." Brad Collins, a fixed income portfolio manager at Vanguard, also expressed confidence in Oracle and the other hyperscalers. "Oracle is most under the microscope, but as a result, has been more diligent in their issuance" so far this year, he said. "Balance sheets are in a healthy starting spot, and [I] would not extrapolate what we are seeing in HY to IG." The company's current troubles could be looked at as a "financing test," said Dynasty Financial Partners' Nerney. They'll either pass or fail, which could mean an additional downgrade, he said. "The real question now is, with the move in rates, how much is that going to cost?" he said. "If rates continue to move higher, just the opportunity cost of investors to hold Oracle paper relative to other things in the market, you're going to see the market demand more." Oracle responded to a request for comment by saying, "We have been very clear that maintaining an investment grade rating is our first priority as a company." "The AI infrastructure business has strong economic returns and we expect it will produce strong free cash flows once projects are ramped," it added. Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical
headlines.summary: Google says its Minnesota AI data center will add clean energy to the grid and protect ratepayers. Experts question whether grid upgrades are needed.
headlines.article_text: How AI data centers are reshaping America's aging grid Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points AI data centers are poised to drive North America’s electricity demand growth over the next decade, fueling a massive grid buildout. Google and Xcel Energy say their proposed 780-megawatt data center in Minnesota will upgrade the grid with cleaner power without shifting infrastructure costs onto existing customers. But experts say much of that buildout could be avoided and warn that utilities have a financial incentive to keep building. In this article GOOGL SPCX XEL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 11:44 11:44 The race to power AI data centers is reshaping America's electric grid Tech If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard. A Gallup survey conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed the construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage. Half of Americans surveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs. Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal with Xcel Energy would add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use. Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power. Google's bet that AI can finance a cleaner grid Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis. Google hopes that its new 780-megawatt data center plan will build goodwill with the Pine Island community and keep the company on track to meet its goal of operating on carbon-free energy, 24 hours a day, seven days a week by 2030 . Google — whose cloud business powers its own Gemini AI and brought in nearly $25 billion in second-quarter revenue, an 82% increase from a year earlier — says it has found a model for doing this the right way. The company plans to finance the addition of 1,400 megawatts of wind, 200 megawatts of solar and 300 megawatts of battery storage to Xcel's grid. Those additions amount to more than the capacity of the data center itself, which Google said is because wind and solar do not generate energy at all times. Xcel Energy said the new power will serve all customers in the local area, not just Google. Xcel also said the upgrades will help advance the local grid's carbon-free energy supply. The proposed agreement between Google and Xcel includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, which Google says will keep the company on the hook for the infrastructure being built on its behalf, even if the AI boom cools. Google will pay for at least 75% of its contracted capacity, even if it uses less, and would owe up to eight years' worth of those minimum demand charges if it terminates the agreement early. "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power," said Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy. "That's where these protections come in." The agreement between Google and Xcel Energy is pending approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. Data centers are driving a historic power buildout New data centers will account for "most" of the projected increase in electricity demand over the next decade, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit regulator. The Department of Energy under President Joe Biden reported that more than 70% of U.S. transmission lines and power transformers were at least 25 years old and found that the cheapest ways of meeting future demand would require the nation's transmission system to more than double in size by 2050 . But hyperscalers argue that they can finance badly needed grid upgrades while also making the grid cleaner and more reliable. "The timing of this industrial revolution couldn't be more perfect," said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of energy and power. "It's right at the time when we needed capital to fix aging infrastructure in the United States." Could data centers use the grid as is? Jigar Shah, a partner at Multiplier, a consulting firm that helps clean energy startups go public, said data center operators could be constructing smaller facilities in places where the grid already has unused capacity. That would minimize the need to build — and pay for — new generation or transmission equipment. "If you fit the load growth that the data centers want into the existing grid, everybody's rates go down by a lot," said Shah. That's because the existing grid has enormous fixed costs from the infrastructure already in place: power plants, transmission lines, substations. If one new customer comes onto the grid and pays a large slice of that, everyone else's bills go down. "And so the question really is, why are people not doing these 25-megawatt data centers? Why are they doing 1,000-megawatt data centers? And it turns out people are just lazy," Shah said. "They're like, well, it's easier for me to contract one data center that's one gigawatt in size than figuring out how to do something on the order of 40 data centers that are 25 megawatts each." Industry watchdogs also warn of another reason that utilities often prefer to build new infrastructure, rather than make more use out of their existing grid. "When [utilities] build something new, they fund part of that investment with dollars from their investors on Wall Street, and they enjoy incredibly high, exorbitant returns on those investments, typically around 10%," said David Pomerantz, executive director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog agency. Building a data center that fits neatly into an existing grid provides little opportunity for a utility to make new money. What if a hyperscaler offers to pay for those grid investments? "One way to leverage data centers to lower people's bills is for data centers to provide that capital at much cheaper rates than the utility," said Pomerantz. "But that's a big problem for the utility. And this fight is actually already emerging." Still, Shah said, the Google/Xcel project in Minnesota is a good example of a data center project acting as a catalyst for newer, greener technology. "Google came in and said, well, here's a new way of doing things, using new technologies. How about we do it that way? And then that helps ratepayers. And the utility was like, yeah, that makes a lot of sense."
